text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate effective temperature and distinguish inference from a theoretical prediction. 01Clarify “surface” and “degrees” The Sun has no solid surface. Its photosphere is the layer from which visible light escapes. Its effective temperature is about 5,772 K, or about 5,500°C. “About 6,000 degrees” is a rough statement; 6,000 K and 6,000°C are different. 02Total power = area × power per unit area F = σSBT4, L = 4πR2σSBTeff4 σSB ≈ 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, distinct from σT. Teff = (L4πR2σSB)1/4 Insert L☉ = 3.828 × 10²⁶ W and R☉ = 6.957 × 10⁸ m to obtain about 5,772 K. Effective temperature means the temperature of a blackbody with the same radius and luminosity, even if the actual spectrum is not exactly blackbody. 03How much of “why” have we answered? Measured luminosity and radius determine effective temperature. Predicting luminosity and radius from mass and composition requires a stellar model combining gravity, nuclear reactions, radiation transport, and convection. A mean free path alone cannot select 6,000 degrees. Inside the Sun, absorption, emission, scattering, and energy transport happen repeatedly. It is insufficient to picture a single core photon merely cooling on its way out. Escape becomes likely where the outward optical depth is of order unity. 04A second thermometer: the spectral shape λmaxT ≈ 2.898 × 10−3 m·K Wien’s displacement law for the peak of the wavelength spectrum Bλ. At 5,772 K the Bλ peak is near 502 nm. The Sun emits a broad spectrum, not just green light. Converting the peak of Bν using c/ν does not give the Bλ peak, because the spectral density is defined per a different variable. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At the same radius, how does effective temperature change if luminosity increases by 16? Show the answer and reasoning It doubles: Teff ∝ L1/4, and the fourth root of 16 is 2.
